steps.text: You just chose one prize over another, and you probably took the rook. [I] Players seem to have turned that feeling into numbers called **counting values**: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The king has no number because it is never taken; it is checkmated. Next comes the table on a board, then a worked capture before any question.

steps.caption: The counting values: pawn 1, knight 3, bishop 3, rook 5, queen 9. The knight and bishop share a number.

claims.statement: A white pawn stands on f2.
A white knight stands on e1.
A white bishop stands on d1.
A white rook stands on c1.
A white queen stands on b1.

steps.caption: A worked example first. White's knight can take an undefended rook. Nothing can take the knight back.

line.say: The knight takes the rook. Nothing guards it, so White wins 5 points and loses nothing.

claims.statement: The knight wins the rook and nothing comes back.
No black piece guards the rook.

steps.caption: Colour makes no difference. Here it is Black's turn, and Black's knight can take a white rook.

line.say: The black knight takes the white rook: Black wins 5 points. The value belongs to the piece, not to its colour.

claims.statement: The black knight wins the rook for nothing.
No white piece guards the rook.

steps.text: Most captures are not free, because the other side can capture back. To judge a capture, **add what you take and subtract what you lose**. The result is the points you gain or lose in the swap. A swap that leaves you ahead is usually a good one when nothing else is going on, even if you lose a piece. Watch three swaps next.

steps.caption: A bishop can take a rook, but a pawn guards it. Add and subtract.

line.say: The bishop takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the bishop back: 3 points out. Five minus three is plus two.

claims.statement: White comes out at least 2 points ahead.
One pawn guards the rook.

steps.caption: Now the other way round. A queen can take a pawn, but a pawn guards it.

line.say: The queen takes the pawn: only 1 point in.
The pawn takes the queen: 9 points out. One minus nine is minus eight.

claims.statement: White ends the swap 8 points down.
The capture is a serious mistake.
One pawn guards the pawn.

steps.caption: A rook can take a rook, and a pawn guards it. Equal pieces cancel out.

line.say: The rook takes the rook: 5 points in.
The pawn takes the rook back: 5 points out. Five minus five is zero: an even swap.

claims.statement: The swap is even.
One pawn guards the rook.

steps.caption: A small piece can take a big one. A pawn can take a knight, even though the queen takes the pawn back.

line.say: The pawn takes the knight: 3 points in.
The queen takes the pawn: 1 point out. Three minus one is plus two.

claims.statement: White nets two points.
One queen guards the knight.

steps.caption: Longer swaps work the same way: keep a running total. A pawn is guarded by a rook, and White has two rooks lined up.

line.say: The first rook takes the pawn: running total plus 1.
The black rook takes it: minus 5, so minus 4.
The second rook takes the rook: plus 5, so plus 1. Black has nothing left to take with.

claims.statement: White nets one point.
One white rook attacks the pawn directly; the other stands behind it.
One black rook guards it.

steps.caption: Count attackers and defenders. White attacks d5 three times and Black guards it twice. The knight goes first: it is the cheapest attacker.

line.say: The knight takes the pawn: 1 in.
The pawn takes the knight: 3 out, running total minus 2.
A rook takes the pawn: 1 in, minus 1.
The black rook takes it: 5 out, minus 6.
The last rook takes the rook: 5 in. White ends one point down.

claims.statement: Two white pieces attack d5 directly; the second rook backs up the first.
Two black pieces guard d5.
The whole sequence ends one point down.

steps.text: **Count, then decide.** List the attackers and defenders of the square, cheapest first. Either side may stop at any moment, so before each capture ask whether it improves your running total; if not, leave the rest. Three attackers against two defenders sounds like a win, yet the board above ends a point down.

steps.title: Same trade, one change
steps.prompt: A rook defended by a pawn is captured. Predict first what the capture does to White's points. Then see what changes when the capturing piece changes, and when only the colours change.

steps.text: Count **points**, not pieces. Giving a rook (5) to win a bishop and a knight (3 and 3) leaves you one point ahead, although you lose one piece and win two. Giving a queen (9) for two minor pieces (6) loses three points, although you win more pieces than you lose. The next board shows how the **order** of the captures changes what you give up.

steps.caption: Two pieces for one. Add the points, not the number of pieces, and send the cheaper piece in first.

line.say: The bishop takes the knight first: 3 points in.
The black bishop takes it back: 3 points out.
The rook takes the bishop: 3 more in. Three minus three plus three is plus three.

claims.statement: Bishop first nets at least three points.
Rook first nets only one point.
The rook and the bishop both attack the knight.
Only the bishop guards the knight.

steps.text: Had the rook gone first, the same exchange would end only one point ahead, because the rook would be the piece Black takes. The cheapest piece goes in first, so the dearest piece is not the one you give up.

steps.caption: Count what each target costs. The queen can take a pawn that is guarded, or a knight that nothing guards.

line.say: The queen takes the knight. Nothing guards it: 3 points in and nothing out.

claims.statement: The loose knight is a free 3 points.
Nothing guards the knight.
Taking the guarded pawn with the queen loses the queen.

steps.text: The numbers are a **rule of thumb**: a good first guide, not a law. They compare swaps when nothing else is going on. Two things can override them: a king with no way out, and a piece that cannot move. Look at both.

steps.caption: Black has a queen and a rook (14 points). White has one rook (5). It is White's move.

line.say: The rook gives checkmate. Black's own pawns block the king's escape, so the extra points are useless.

claims.statement: The rook move is checkmate.
The rook can reach e8.

steps.text: **Checkmate ends the game** whatever the points say. A quick mate can come from a position that looks lost on the count.

steps.caption: [H] The rook is worth 5 and the bishop 3, yet the rook is shut in by its own knight and pawn. Here one knight move frees it, so this board only shows the mechanism: a piece that cannot move does less than its number says.

claims.statement: The white rook has no legal move.
The black bishop has 13 legal moves.
The engine still rates White clearly better, because one move frees the rook.

steps.caption: The reverse can happen too. A pawn is worth 1, but this one is one step from the last row and nothing can stop it.

line.say: The pawn reaches the last row and becomes a queen: its 1 point has just become 9.

claims.statement: The pawn can promote on a8.
With a queen soon, White is far ahead.

steps.text: Where do the numbers come from? [H] A guess: players wanted a sum they could do in their head, and the table fits that, since a queen is close to a rook plus a minor piece plus a pawn (9 against 5, 3 and 1). [S] Capablanca (1921) compared pieces in pairs, for example a rook as a minor piece plus about two pawns. [S] Edward Lasker (1915) saw how freely a piece can move as its real value.

Two honest limits. [I] A bishop and a knight share a number but are not identical: a bishop tends to be stronger in open positions, a knight in closed ones. [I] A common habit is to trade pieces when ahead in points and avoid trades when behind, because the lead becomes a larger share of what is left.
